external_sources.title: MoneyHelper Budget planner
external_sources.supports: A budget compares money in and spending over the same period. Classroom amounts are fictional; pupils do not open accounts or disclose finances.

external_sources.title: GOV.UK Accepting returns and giving refunds: the law
external_sources.supports: Faulty goods and an in-shop change of mind are different. A change of mind alone does not create a legal refund right for ordinary goods bought in person. Proof of purchase can take more than one form. Specific remedies depend on the facts; no automatic refund promise is made.

external_sources.title: National Careers Service Explore careers
external_sources.supports: Job profiles help check tasks, skills, entry requirements and possible routes. Classroom role cards are simplified authored examples, not quotations or guarantees of entry.

external_sources.title: HSE Introduction to managing health and safety
external_sources.supports: Employers must provide suitable information, training and supervision for safe work. A new worker should ask for instruction rather than attempt unfamiliar equipment.

external_sources.title: PSHE Association Handling complex issues safely
external_sources.supports: Use ground rules, fictional scenarios, the right to pass and the setting safeguarding response.

vocab.definition: A plan for money in and money out.
Money needed to buy or pay for something.
Something a person needs for their situation.
Something we would like to have.
A person who buys goods or services.

cases.text: Rae has £15. Travel costs £4 and lunch costs £5. A book costs £3.
cases.fact: The total cost is £12. There is £3 left.
cases.next_step: Check that all needed costs are covered.
cases.staff_note: £4 + £5 + £3 = £12; £15 − £12 = £3. A need depends on the person and context.

cases.text: Lee has £10. Travel costs £4 and lunch costs £5. Lee wants a £4 game.
cases.fact: All three cost £13, which is £3 over the amount.
cases.next_step: Wait for the game or change the plan without losing needed travel or food.
cases.staff_note: Needs use £9, leaving £1. Avoid judging someone for having little money.

cases.text: Jo buys a new bag from a shop. Its zip is faulty. Jo has proof of purchase.
cases.fact: The new bag has a fault.
cases.next_step: Tell the seller about the fault and ask for a remedy.
cases.staff_note: Faulty goods may lead to a refund, repair or replacement depending on the facts. Do not teach that every return guarantees a refund.

cases.text: Kit buys a sound blue bag in a shop. Later, Kit wants red. There is no fault.
cases.fact: This is a change of mind after buying in person.
cases.next_step: Ask about the shop’s returns policy.
cases.staff_note: For ordinary in-shop purchases a change of mind alone does not create a legal refund right. A shop may offer a policy. Online buying has different rules.

cases.text: A site shows a £6 price. Kim has £8. The delivery cost is not shown yet.
cases.next_step: Check the total with delivery before choosing.
cases.staff_note: Do not open a live shopping site or enter payment details. The fictional price is not a current market quote.

cases.text: A new torch is faulty. Ali lost the receipt but has other proof of purchase.
cases.fact: There is a fault and other proof may be available.
cases.next_step: Ask the seller what proof they can accept.
cases.staff_note: A receipt is useful but is not the only possible proof of purchase. Do not ask pupils to show real bank records.

slides.notes:
PSHE-LAUNCH-A2-W01 · Tuesday 3–Friday 6 November 2026
We Do: 5 minutes.
Teacher: Read A/B/C aloud and ask for a letter plus a reason. B. A faulty item can give the buyer rights to a remedy. Ask the seller to deal with the fault and keep proof of purchase. The remedy depends on the facts. A denies rights; C wrongly treats all returns alike. Contrast a sound item bought in a shop that the buyer simply no longer likes. Reteach with one fresh example if the distinction is missed.
TA: offer processing time, read or scribe exact words; record support without supplying the assessed answer.

Purpose and success checks
How can a money plan help us choose?
I can plan spending within a set amount. I can spot a fault or a change of mind. I can explain a sensible next step.
LAUNCH-PSHE-W1-E1: Individual one-day budget calculation and consumer-rights scenario response, with a reason, next step and response after feedback.
Before pupils arrive

Prepare the deck, Evidence Sheet and Vocabulary Mat for each learner; one set of Support Cards; pens, timer and spare paper. Have counters and a calculator for the fictional budget. Read the Staff Answers. No log-ins, live transactions, employer contact or web search is needed.

Identify the staff member and agreed place for private help. Read the local safeguarding route. Offer a quiet seat, processing time and a supported break. Pupils may work alongside each other or with an adult; capture each person’s own evidence.
Calendar
W1 starts Tuesday 3 November: Monday 2 November is a training day. No fixed lesson day or clock slot was supplied. Enter the actual teaching date above; do not assume a Monday lesson in W1.

Hinge and reteach

B. A faulty item can give the buyer rights to a remedy. Ask the seller to deal with the fault and keep proof of purchase. The remedy depends on the facts. A denies rights; C wrongly treats all returns alike. Contrast a sound item bought in a shop that the buyer simply no longer likes. If the reason is missing, re-model the key distinction and try a fresh case. A correct letter alone is not evidence of understanding.
Access routes

Supported: use counters or a calculator; read cases C and D aloud. Complete both budget and rights parts with pointing or scribing. Independent: calculate the budget, consider all six cases and explain a consumer choice. Aspire: explain how a missing cost or a different purchase fact changes the choice.

Begin evidence during the 12-minute practice; use the six-minute capture to finish it. Accept pointing, speech, drawing or writing. Read and scribe without supplying the assessed reason. No forced pair work, cold calling or public performance.
Safe discussion evidence and learner voice
Boundaries and private help

Use only the printed fictional amounts. Calculators and counters are allowed; record their use. Do not ask about pocket money, debt, family income or purchases. Do not collect receipts or account details. Teach the next step, not individual financial or legal advice.

Keep cases fictional and allow a pass or a private alternative. If a concern arises, listen calmly, do not investigate in class or promise secrecy, and follow local safeguarding procedures. Keep safeguarding records separate from learning evidence. Help the learner reach another trusted adult if needed.
Assessment and feedback

Ari: £18 in; bus £4 + lunch £6 = £10 needed; £8 left. Adding a £5 magazine gives £15 total spending and £3 left. Without the magazine, £8 remains. Either choice is acceptable with a reason. Rights evidence must distinguish a fault from a change of mind and name the seller/help route.

Retain the actual working, reason, response mode and support. A copied model or blank form is not completed evidence. Use VF · WS · I · NS+ (Yellow Box) · // (self-edit) · ? (read back) · R (responded) · E (evidence in the school's evidence record). R requires Voice, Audience, an NS+ prompt and the learner’s response in their own colour. Record E only when evidence has actually been banked.
Lundy moments

Space: a calm, non-personal way to respond. Voice: choose a view and explain it. Audience: the teaching adult listens or reads, then replies. Influence: record the learner’s requested support or next task and what changes as a result.
Speaking listening and writing

Possible communication evidence: explain a spending choice, listen to a different reason and write or dictate a calm message about a faulty item. The receiving teacher maps authentic responses to their own portfolio requirements. No communication criteria are assigned here.

Teacher model and hinge
Sam has £20 for one day. Bus: £6. Lunch: £5. Needs cost £11. There is £9 left. A book costs £7. It would leave £2. Headphones cost £12. That is £3 too much. Sam can wait and keep money for the bus.

B. A faulty item can give the buyer rights to a remedy. Ask the seller to deal with the fault and keep proof of purchase. The remedy depends on the facts. A denies rights; C wrongly treats all returns alike. Contrast a sound item bought in a shop that the buyer simply no longer likes.
Individual evidence key

Ari: £18 in; bus £4 + lunch £6 = £10 needed; £8 left. Adding a £5 magazine gives £15 total spending and £3 left. Without the magazine, £8 remains. Either choice is acceptable with a reason. Rights evidence must distinguish a fault from a change of mind and name the seller/help route.
Feedback and safe teaching
Case A: £4 + £5 + £3 = £12; £15 − £12 = £3. A need depends on the person and context.
Case B: Needs use £9, leaving £1. Avoid judging someone for having little money.
Case C: Faulty goods may lead to a refund, repair or replacement depending on the facts. Do not teach that every return guarantees a refund.
Case D: For ordinary in-shop purchases a change of mind alone does not create a legal refund right. A shop may offer a policy. Online buying has different rules.
Case E: Do not open a live shopping site or enter payment details. The fictional price is not a current market quote.
Case F: A receipt is useful but is not the only possible proof of purchase. Do not ask pupils to show real bank records.
Common misunderstandings

A need is contextual, not a judgement about a family. Money left is not the same as income. A budget may reveal a shortfall that needs help; it does not create extra money. Consumer rights do not mean every unwanted purchase gets a refund.
Teaching boundary

Use only the printed fictional amounts. Calculators and counters are allowed; record their use. Do not ask about pocket money, debt, family income or purchases. Do not collect receipts or account details. Teach the next step, not individual financial or legal advice.
Response and next teaching step

If the reason is vague, return to the case words or working. If a fact is missing, ask what must be checked and with whom. Re-model one new example, then retain the learner’s own revision. Use the NS+ prompt and learner response in their own colour before recording R. E means evidence actually banked in the school's evidence record, not a promise to upload.
Private help and assessment boundary

Identify the school support route. Listen without investigating in class; never promise secrecy. Use the local safeguarding procedure, separate from lesson evidence.
